title: Al-Kahf, part one
tomorrow: why would a wise man hole a poor family's boat?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yusuf's story in one sitting, ending with a brother who could have punished and said instead: no blame on you today. Now a new surah, and more young people in trouble.
screen: `NO BLAME ON YOU TODAY.` → `MORE YOUNG PEOPLE IN TROUBLE.`

segments.voice: Finals week. Somebody in every group chat deletes their apps and announces cave mode. The Qur'an has a cave too, and the people in it are young. A few young men in a city that pressed them to give up their faith slip out toward the hills. They have no plan past the mouth of a cave. At the entrance they stop and pray, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! Give us mercy from Thy presence, and shape for us right conduct in our plight." Then they go in, and they sleep.
screen: `CAVE MODE.` → `YOUNG MEN, NO PLAN.` → `MERCY, AND RIGHT CONDUCT.`

segments.voice: Al-Kahf tells it like a dream. The sun slides past the cave's mouth. Their dog lies with his paws stretched across the threshold. When they wake, they guess they've slept a day, or part of one. One of them walks into town with their silver coin to buy food, and the world has moved on without them. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the surah lets people argue over how many sleepers there were, then sets the argument down. Only God knows their number, it says, so don't quarrel about it. The count was never the point. The prayer at the door was. Then, in the same reading, a second picture: a man with two gardens of vines and date palms and a stream between, so sure of them he can't imagine them ever perishing. His friend answers: "If only, when thou enteredst thy garden, thou hadst said: That which Allah willeth (will come to pass)! There is no strength save in Allah!" Then the fruit is ruined, and he's left wringing his hands over everything he spent. Two pictures side by side. Young men with nothing, who ask for mercy and are kept. A man with everything, who forgets whose strength it was. The cave isn't a hideout. It's a place where you're held for a while, and from which you walk back out. A report some scholars accept speaks of a light between two Fridays for whoever reads this surah, which is why some Muslims read it every Friday.
screen: `YOUNG, WITH NOTHING, AT A CAVE.` · `NOBODY NEEDS THE COUNT.` · `A MAN TOO SURE OF HIS GARDEN.` · `KEPT, NOT HIDDEN.` · then, large: `THE CAVE.`

segments.voice: Say the young men's line out loud, slowly: our Lord, give us mercy from Thy presence, and shape for us right conduct in our plight. If it's your prayer, say it as one; if not, hear it as theirs. Then let the sit be a cave: not a place to hide from your week, a place to be held in it.
screen: `SAY IT ONCE, OUT LOUD.` · `HELD, NOT HIDING.`

howItsDone: Some Muslims read Surah al-Kahf on Fridays, following a report about a light between two Fridays; it is read aloud in Arabic or quietly from a copy or a phone.

fork.setup: your cousin's food truck is booming and he posts that nothing can stop him now. his friend wants to say something. what fits the garden story?
options: warn him the truck will fail, like the garden did.
remind him gently whose strength it is: what Allah wills.
tell him wealth itself is the problem and he should sell.
fork.reveal: the friend in the story doesn't curse the garden or the money. he says what the owner forgot: that which Allah wills; there is no strength save in Allah.

original.note: Arabic: the cave. the surah takes its name from the young men's refuge.

Amira arc (1583–1596), day 1: Amira is near the end of senior year and leaves for college in the fall. Dadi Fatima asks to read al-Kahf with her every Friday 'before you go'; Amira, in finals, wants to go 'cave mode'. The arc runs through her dad Yusuf giving her summer shifts at the coffee shop to Bilal, a new hire (1584), finding out why (1587, 1590), a rude customer and Jordan's grandmother (1588, the unity beat), talking it out with Yusuf (1589–1590), reading Ya-Sin with Dadi for Auntie Nasreen (1591), and the worry of leaving Dadi (1594).
